newsitem.title: USA: Treasury proposes money laundering rules for non-banks.
newsitem.headline: Treasury proposes money laundering rules for non-banks.

text.p: With illicit money laundering moving from highly regulated banks to local check cashing outlets and services that send money by wire, the Treasury Department proposed on Monday new reporting rules for non-bank transactions.

Money laundering is the "life blood of organised crime," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said at a news briefing here. "But it is also the 'Achilles heel,' as it gives us a way to attack the leaders of criminal organisations."
Under the proposal, money transmitters, which send money by wire, will have to report all transfers of more than $750 out of the United States.
Such money transmitters transfer about $11 billion a year, both within and outside of the country, usually in amounts of less than $500, Treasury officials said.
A broader array of money service businesses, including firms that issue money orders or travellers checks, will have to register with the government and report suspicious activity as banks do now.

Under Secretary of Enforcement Raymond Kelly, who is a former New York City police chief, said the new $750 reporting requirement was based on a successful programme in the New York City area that was known as Operation El Dorado.

"We estimated that 12 transmitters in Queens County alone sent $800 million to Colombia each year," Kelly told reporters. "To account for this money legitimately, each Colombian household in the area would have had to wire $30,000, an amount which exceeds the average annual income in this community by $3,000."
So federal officials required the transmitters to report all transfer to Colombia over $750.
"The results were immediate and dramatic," Kelly said. Money launders were forced to smuggle cash out of the city, leading to seizures of $50 million in eastern ports, he said.

The rules "are needed and they make sense," Representative Henry Gonzalez, Deomocrat of Texas, said in a statement. "The lesson learned from the Texas border experience is that strong but reasonable regulatory oversight of a vulnerable financial segment can go a long way in interrupting, and shutting down, a money laundering pipeline."
The proposal was issued for comment for 90 days and should be enacted in final form by the end of the year, Kelly said.
